Getting Started > Haxe Compilation Backend: Can SA Become Haxe's Low-Level Compiler?
Status: discussion finalized (2026-10-28). Conclusion: yes, but the correct form is neither modifying the Haxe compiler nor source-to-source transpilation; it is HashLink bytecode translation (hl2sa). The real cost center is "runtime porting" such as the GC runtime and the exception mechanism, not the compiler itself. Not proposed as a project; the probe design is ready.

1. First, Disambiguate the Question: Three Routes to "Becoming a Haxe Backend"

"SA becomes Haxe's low-level compiler" has three completely different meanings, with costs differing by an order of magnitude:

RouteFormFrontend (syntax/types/macros)Assessment
A. A compiler generatorAdd an SA code generator inside the Haxe compiler (OCaml), alongside genhxcpp and the likeDone for free by the Haxe compilerThe most "orthodox", but it means following the upstream OCaml codebase long-term, and writing the entire Haxe runtime from scratch on SA; the highest upstream merge cost
B. HashLink bytecode translation (hl2sa)Haxe → HashLink bytecode → SA; the translator is isomorphic to bc2saDone for free by the Haxe compilerRecommended. HL is itself a register-based, strongly typed low-level bytecode, the closest in shape to SA among all candidates; it touches neither OCaml nor source semantics
C. Via a C/C++ intermediatehxcpp's C++ or HL/C's C → LLVM bitcode → bc2saDone for free by the Haxe compilerLooks ready-made but is actually the most blocked: C++ exceptions, the hxcpp runtime, and setjmp/longjmp are all outside bc2sa's current coverage, and there is no sweet spot like the Rust route's panic=abort + no_std

Relation to the earlier discussion of 2026-10-27: what was rejected then was "Haxe source transpiled to SA" (the haxe2sa source route) — the source layer would have to replicate all of Haxe's semantics and is comprehensively dominated by the bc2sa route; that conclusion stands. What this page asks about is "serving as the compilation backend", where the frontend semantics are entirely borne by the Haxe compiler; the nature of the question is completely different, and so is the conclusion.

2. There Are Only One and a Half Semantic Gaps

1. GC vs Ownership (the Only Real Gap)

Haxe is a GC language (object graphs can form cycles; Dynamic can reference anything), while SA is an ownership/capability model with no GC. This is not a principled obstacle: SA is a low-level target language, and a GC runtime can perfectly well be implemented on top of it — hxcpp (the C++ target) itself ships a GC runtime, and the HashLink VM is itself a mark-and-sweep GC. The real costs are two: ① Haxe programs cannot enjoy SA's ownership dividends (no GC pauses, deterministic release), and the compiled output always carries a GC with it; ② the GC runtime enters the TCB and must be maintained by us. The choice: reference counting fits SA's ownership shape better (deterministic release, small implementation), but Haxe object graphs can form cycles, so it needs cycle collection to back it up, or a switch to mark-and-sweep; HashLink natively uses mark-and-sweep. To be decided empirically in the P1 phase: start with reference counting, and register the cycle problem explicitly rather than pretending it does not exist.

2. Exceptions (Half a Gap)

Haxe exceptions are real control flow, and HL bytecode has corresponding Trap/Throw-style opcodes; SA has no native exception mechanism. The countermeasure is to solve it at the runtime layer: a handler chain + a cross-frame jump primitive (sa_std just needs one small setjmp-family primitive, the same class of small std surface item as the "missing raw socket primitive" registered by the BE line), or a whole-call-graph status-code protocol (highly intrusive; not taken). We cannot dodge it the way the Rust route does with panic=abort — Haxe programs genuinely depend on try/catch semantics.

3. Everything Else Is Not a Gap, Just Engineering Volume

Closures, enums (algebraic data types), anonymous structures, iterators, containers such as strings/arrays/Maps, and Dynamic and reflection (Type/Reflect): HL bytecode has directly corresponding low-level operations for all of them (ToDyn, DynField, closure and enum-constructor opcodes, etc.); the translator maps them one by one + the runtime provides a layer of dynamic value representation (a tagged union + a type registry). Haxe macros are executed by the Haxe compiler itself at compile time, and the backend is not involved at all — this is the biggest bargain of "serving as a backend" compared with "source transpilation".

3. Why HL's Shape Fits SA Best

  • HL is register-based bytecode: functions, registers, basic blocks, and an explicit calling convention — the same family as SA's register model; the phi cross-block reuse wall that bc2sa hit on the LLVM route, should it appear on the HL route too, already has a proven solution of the same kind (cross-block slot publication + reloading in the use block).
  • HL is strongly typed bytecode (type tags such as Int/Float/Bool/Dyn/Obj/Enum/Fun follow the instructions), so translation does not need to rebuild type inference.
  • Passing aggregate values (objects/enum constructors) can follow the slot model + sret convention already landed by bc2sa.
  • bc2sa's probe verdict can be reused directly as methodology: first census the opcode coverage (bc2sa's three sample tiers hit only 9 classes of construct), then fill in class by class, rather than writing a big translator first.

4. Value and Positioning

If it succeeds, Haxe brings a mature language frontend + macro system + cross-platform ecosystem (OpenFL/Kha and the like on the game side, and many pure-logic libraries), and SA gains "the first mature frontend borrowed through a shell, besides SLA/slars"; the Haxe side gains a backend that produces native binaries and can enter SA's capability/permission system. Division of labor with the two existing lines: slars is our own hand-written frontend, bc2sa is the channel for machine-converting real Rust, and hl2sa is the channel for borrowing a mature ecosystem's shell — none of the three replaces another.

5. Phases (Probe First, the Same Play as bc2sa)

  • P0 probe (week-scale): directly translate an HL bytecode subset (scalar operations, function calls, closures, enums, arrays) to SA → sa check/build → compare item by item against native HashLink runs; at the same time, census the coverage of all HL opcodes (four classes: has an equivalent / directly mappable / needs runtime modeling / model does not fit, following the eight-language-family census criteria).
  • P1, three runtime pieces: empirical GC choice (reference counting first + cycle cases compared), the exception Trap mechanism (handler chain + jump primitive), and the Dynamic representation and type registry.
  • P2, sweet-spot census: census the surface of the Haxe standard library and mainstream pure-logic libraries to fix the first runnable scope (pure logic first, IO/platform libraries later); acceptance follows the bc2sa criteria: a real Haxe program compared end to end against a native HashLink run.

6. Risk Register

  • The GC runtime enters the TCB together with the SA compiler/referee: the SAB referee misjudgments proven by the AW line (structs with multiple String fields) show that compiler maturity itself is a shared risk of shell-borrowing routes like this one, so referee misjudgments must be listed as acceptance items already in the probe phase.
  • Following cost: the HL bytecode format evolves with HashLink versions, so the translator must pin a version and write the version wall into the prerequisites (bc2sa's LLVM version wall is a ready lesson).
  • Ecosystem size: the Haxe community is smaller than Rust/TS; the benefit ceiling of this route depends on the user's actual need for the Haxe ecosystem, so investing beyond P1 in advance is inadvisable.
  • This page is only a finalized discussion; the project has not been proposed or scheduled; whether to propose it is the user's call.
